summary: Extends the MPLS architecture, which originally had only downstream-assigned labels, with upstream-assigned labels. It describes the procedures for upstream label assignment and introduces the Context-Specific Label Space. This helps for things like multicast where the sender, rather than the receiver, may best choose the label. It has been updated since.

plainLanguage.summary: Usually the receiver picks the name tag for incoming packages. Here the sender can pick it instead, and a special area keeps those tags from clashing.

questions: what is mpls upstream label assignment
what is a context label in mpls
what is the difference between upstream and downstream assigned labels
subtitle: How an MPLS router can choose a label itself and tell its neighbors, using a separate label space to avoid clashes.

tldr.problem: The MPLS architecture in RFC 3031 only allows downstream-assigned labels, where the receiving router picks the label. That does not suit cases such as one sender reaching several receivers at once.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5331 adds upstream-assigned labels, chosen by the sending router, and a Context-Specific Label Space in which the receiver looks them up. On a LAN, a context label identifies the sender.
tldr.outcome: MPLS gains a way to use upstream-assigned labels, with MPLS multicast as the example use. RFC 7274 updates this document.

today: RFC 5331 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7274. It leaves the label distribution protocol mechanisms to other documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3031 limits the MPLS architecture to downstream-assigned labels. It says the decision to bind a label to a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) is made by the Label Switching Router (LSR) that is downstream with respect to that binding, which then tells the upstream LSR. Label bindings are distributed from downstream to upstream.

This document introduces upstream-assigned labels and the procedures for assigning them. RFC 3031 describes per-platform and per-interface label spaces; this document generalizes the per-interface one into a Context-Specific Label Space and describes a Neighbor Label Space as an example. Upstream-assigned labels are always looked up in a context-specific label space.
sections.plainLanguage: In the old way the person receiving a parcel decides what label it carries. This document lets the sender choose the label too.

sections.title: Context-Specific Label Space
sections.content:
An LSR may keep one or more context-specific label spaces. In general, labels MUST be looked up in the per-platform label space unless something about the context says a label must be looked up in a particular context-specific space. The per-interface label space from RFC 3031 is one example: the receiving interface is the context.

With upstream-assigned labels, the context is provided by the LSR that assigns the label. Two examples are given: a tunnel over which packets arrive, where the top label after decapsulation is looked up in a space specific to the root of the tunnel, and the neighbor that sent the packet. If the tunnel is an MPLS tunnel, penultimate-hop-popping (PHP) MUST be disabled for it, so the receiver can tell which tunnel the packet came over.

The RFC also defines a context label: a label that identifies a label table in which the label immediately below it should be looked up. A context label carried as the outermost label over a multi-access subnet or tunnel MUST be unique within that subnet or tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine each sender has its own separate list of name tags. The receiver checks the right list depending on who the package came from.

sections.title: Upstream and Downstream Assignment
sections.content:
Take two adjacent LSRs, Ru (upstream) and Rd (downstream), that have agreed to bind label L to FEC F. If Rd made the binding and advertised it to Ru, it is downstream-assigned. If Ru made it and advertised it to Rd, it is upstream-assigned. A binding made by a third party and advertised to both is also called upstream-assigned.

An upstream-assigned label at the top of the stack must be looked up by an LSR other than the one that assigned it, so it MUST always be looked up in a context-specific label space. No coordination is required between upstream and downstream assignments: a label value may be upstream-assigned to one FEC and downstream-assigned to another.

Using upstream-assigned labels is an OPTIONAL feature, and they MUST NOT be used unless it is known that the downstream LSR supports them. For a given pair of adjacent LSRs on an LSP for a FEC, either Ru distributes an upstream-assigned binding or Rd distributes a downstream-assigned one, but NOT both. An application that needs upstream-assigned labels MUST say so explicitly; otherwise downstream assignment is assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever names the label depends on the job. Most of the time the receiver names it, but a sender can name it when that works better, as long as the receiver is ready for that.

sections.title: Assigning and Distributing Labels
sections.content:
The only requirement on an upstream LSR is that an upstream-assigned label be unambiguous in the context-specific label space in which the downstream LSR will look it up. An LSR that is the head end of multiple tunnels SHOULD, by default, assign the labels for all LSPs carried over those tunnels from a single label space common to the tunnels, and SHOULD use the same IP address as the head identifier of the tunnels.

No entry is created in the Incoming Label Map (ILM) at the upstream LSR, because these are not incoming labels. An upstream label is an outgoing label for the upstream LSR, so it is part of a Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) that imposes the label on the packet.

Distribution needs a label distribution protocol to carry the binding from upstream to downstream. It resembles ordered or independent LSP control for downstream-assigned labels. Under ordered control, an LSR distributes an upstream-assigned binding for a FEC if it is the ingress, if it already received an upstream label binding from its adjacent upstream LSR, or if it received a request for a downstream label binding from its upstream neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender writes the tag on its own outgoing packages, so it keeps the tag in its list of things to stick on, not in its list of tags to look for.

sections.title: The Upstream Neighbor Label Space
sections.content:
If the top label of a packet being processed by Rd is upstream-assigned, it is looked up in a context-specific label space, not in the per-platform one. Rd keeps a separate ILM for Ru's context-specific label space and reserves in it the labels Ru assigns. Rd MUST be able to tell whether the top label is upstream-assigned and what the context is, and how it does so depends on how Ru sends the packet.

If Ru uses an IP or MPLS tunnel, Rd learns this from the tunnel the packet arrives on, and Rd MUST use a separate label space for each unique tunnel root. The root is identified by the head-end IP address. For an MPLS tunnel, Rd takes the context from the labels above L in the stack. For an IP/GRE tunnel, the context comes from the source address in the IP header. For point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint tunnels one node can always be identified as the root; for a tunnel set up by configuration, the root address must be configured; for a GRE tunnel that needs no setup, the root is the source address of the encapsulated packets.

If Ru and Rd share a multi-access data link, whether L is upstream-assigned is shown by a different ether type in the frame (per RFC 5332). To give the context as well, Ru encapsulates the packet in a one-hop MPLS tunnel using a context label that Ru assigned, with L as the second label in the stack.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver keeps one tag list per sender. It works out who sent the package from the road it arrived on, or from a special outer tag, and then reads the right list.

sections.title: Context Labels on LANs
sections.content:
For a labeled packet with the upstream label assignment ether type, the top label is the context. The upstream LSR assigns it and advertises it to downstream LSRs. A context label for a LAN interface MUST be unique across all context labels assigned by other LSRs on that LAN, and received context labels MUST be looked up in the context of the LAN interface they arrived on.

Two ways to choose one are given. First, each LSR is provisioned with a 20-bit context label per LAN interface, and the provisioning system keeps them unique. Second, labels can be auto-generated when each LSR on the LAN has an IPv4 primary address: if the network mask is greater than 12 bits, the remaining 20 bits of host part map to a unique label. To avoid the reserved label range, the host part is offset by 0x10, and host values greater than 0xFFFEF are not allowed. If any LSR on the LAN has only IPv6 addresses, the first method is used.

Two upstream routers on different LANs may end up with the same context label value, but that causes no ambiguity because the lookup is per LAN interface.
sections.plainLanguage: On a shared street, each sender gets its own street-sign number that nobody else on that street uses. Two different streets can reuse the same number.

sections.title: Use Case: MPLS Multicast
sections.content:
The typical use is MPLS multicast. An upstream LSR Ru is adjacent to several downstream LSRs on an LSP and is connected to them over a multi-access medium or tunnel, and Ru wants to send a single copy of a packet to all of them.

Over a tunnel, Ru distributes an upstream-assigned label L bound to the FEC to all the downstream LSRs and sends a packet with top label L on the tunnel. Over a multi-access medium, the packet's top label is the context label that identifies Ru and the label below it is L. Each downstream LSR interprets the packet in the context of Ru. All of them MUST therefore support an Upstream Neighbor Label Space for Ru. How this is determined is specific to the application and out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If one sender wants to shout the same news to a whole room, it can use one tag that everyone in the room understands, so it only has to send one copy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for upstream-assigned and context labels are no different in kind than those for downstream-assigned labels. Procedures for distributing such labels are out of scope, so their security considerations are not covered.

There is one specific risk in the auto-generated LAN context label procedure. It assumes the IP addresses of all LSR interfaces on the LAN are unique in their low-order 20 bits. If two LSRs with the same low-order 20 bits are placed on the LAN, other LSRs are likely to misroute packets sent to the LAN by either of them. The RFC points to a separate security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks for wider discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Mostly the risks are the same as before. The one new trap is two senders ending up with the same street-sign number, which makes packages go to the wrong place.

left.title: Downstream-assigned
left.desc: Rd binds label L to FEC F and advertises the binding to Ru. This is the only kind RFC 3031 covers.

right.title: Upstream-assigned
right.desc: Ru binds label L to FEC F and advertises it to Rd, which looks it up in a context-specific label space.
